lines: The US team takes the shop's entire events lake and replicates all of it over to the EU, purely for performance, over one single weekend.
Come Monday morning, the privacy officer asks a genuinely uncomfortable question: which EU customers' data is now sitting in the United States?
Separately, and completely unrelated, the EU region's own catalog database fails outright, and the replicated buckets turn out to hold no usable table metadata at all.
Two decisions, each made back at design time, would have prevented both of these problems.
Which two, and roughly what does each one actually cost to put in place?
answer: The privacy problem was never really about speed at all; it was about which rows were allowed to cross that border in the first place, so a faster replication tool fixes absolutely nothing.
What actually would have helped is a per-dataset residency rule for the first problem, and a catalog backup-and-restore plan folded into failover for the second.

lines: Every single dataset gets tagged by its own classification first.
EU personal data simply stops dead at the border, like a closed gate it can't pass through.
A de-identified aggregate, by contrast, crosses that same border completely freely, and global reference data just starts out present on both sides at once.
Replicating a dataset costs its own size, multiplied by the egress rate, every single day it keeps running.
Federating a query instead costs nothing standing still, but every individual query still has to cross that border on its own.
Priced out against this shop's own real volumes, which path actually turns out cheaper depends entirely on the query itself.
So replicate the de-identified aggregate only, and never the underlying rows themselves.
A paid, SLA-backed replication service bounds that lag down to minutes, which is a real, known cost traded for a real, known promise, not some unbounded best-effort copy.
Now picture an entire region going down.
The bucket itself survives just fine, since it was already being replicated.
The catalog database, the encryption keys, and every pipeline's own checkpoints do not survive, because bucket replication never touched a single one of them.
Orders, events, and aggregates each get their own named recovery point and their own recovery time, stated plainly up front.
That's baked into the design from the start, never something bolted on only after the failover plan already got built.
Regional partials for something like "global revenue" all combine together into one single figure.
That combined figure is only ever as fresh as its single slowest region's most recent update, and this design states that plainly instead of hiding it behind one clean-looking number.
A placement gate, organized by dataset tag. A priced decision between replicating and federating.
A failover plan that genuinely covers the catalog and the keys, not merely the bucket on its own.
And one single global number that stays honest about exactly which region it's still waiting on.
One more, to really use this for real: the shop opens up a brand-new third region.
A query now needs "global revenue including the new region" at the exact same minute that new region's own pipeline is still backfilling its very first week of history.
What should that number actually say in the meantime?
answer: Blending that region's partial, still-catching-up numbers straight in, left completely unmarked, breaks the whole stalest-region promise by hiding exactly which part of the figure hasn't caught up yet.
Excluding that new region from the figure for now, and simply saying so plainly, keeps the number honest about what it does and doesn't yet cover.
